statement: A translator should acquire a systematic theoretical understanding of language rather than rely on intuition and practice alone, so that translation decisions can be reflected on and justified.

The value of theoretical knowledge for a translator is that it minimizes the risk on any given task, prepares the practitioner for the unpredictable, and supports confident, knowledge-based decisions instead of hunches.
Weighing the advantages and disadvantages of alternative renderings is impossible without a thorough, intimate knowledge of language, the translator's raw material.
Theoretical knowledge of translation has no value unless it is grounded in practical experience.
condition: only when applied together with practical translating experience

statement: A translator should be able to stand back and reflect on what they do and how they do it, demonstrating deliberate control rather than reliance on an unexplained flair for translation.
A translator needs a sound knowledge of the raw material of the craft: what language is and how it comes to function for its users.
Modern linguistics, including text linguistics and pragmatics, studies language in use and offers translators valuable insight into the nature and function of language.
Equivalence in translation can usually be obtained only to some extent and is always relative, because it is influenced by a variety of linguistic and cultural factors.
The term equivalence is adopted as a convenience familiar to translators rather than as a concept with established theoretical status.

Dividing language into discrete areas such as words, grammar, and text is an analytical convenience rather than a real boundary; the areas are not discrete and it is virtually impossible to say where one ends and another begins.

A translation decision taken at the level of a word or grammatical category is influenced by the perceived function and purpose of both source and target text and has implications for the discourse as a whole.
Because meaning is realized through form, a translator cannot interpret a text's overall meaning without first understanding the meanings of its individual words, phrases, and grammatical structures.

Both top-down (text-to-sign) and bottom-up (word-to-text) approaches to analysing translation are valid; the top-down approach is theoretically stronger but harder to follow for those without linguistic training.
Translation strategies should be understood as actual options observed in authentic translated texts, not as preconceived ideal or correct solutions to be applied mechanically.
Except in extreme cases it is virtually impossible to draw a clear line between a good and a bad translation; every translation has strengths and weaknesses and is open to improvement.
exception: extreme cases where a translation is clearly wrong

statement: A back-translation renders a target text as literally as the point requires to expose its morphological, syntactic, or lexical structure; it gives insight into structure but is never equivalent to the original and is a theoretically unsound but necessary compromise.

Despite theoretical arguments that translation is impossible because languages are never sufficiently similar and reality is not independent of language, translation remains a necessary and valuable activity that connects cultures.
Languages are not nomenclatures: each language articulates and organizes the world differently and does not simply attach names to a set of universal, pre-existing concepts.

There is no one-to-one correspondence between orthographic words and elements of meaning within or across languages, so one word in one language may correspond to several words in another and vice versa.

The morpheme is the minimal formal element of meaning and cannot be analysed further, whereas a word may contain several morphemes; keeping this distinction in mind is useful in translation, particularly when dealing with neologisms in the source language.

The lexical meaning of a word is the specific value it holds within a particular linguistic system; it is rarely possible to analyse a word cleanly into fully distinct components of meaning because language is too complex.
Following Cruse, meaning in words and utterances can be analysed into four types: propositional, expressive, presupposed, and evoked meaning.

Propositional meaning is the relation between a word and what it refers to and is the basis on which an utterance is judged true or false; when a translation is called inaccurate, it is usually the propositional meaning being questioned.

Expressive meaning relates to the speaker's feelings or attitude and cannot be judged true or false, so two words can share the same propositional meaning yet differ in expressive meaning, both within one language and across languages.

Expressive difference between near-synonyms is often a matter of degree of forcefulness rather than mere presence or absence of an attitude, as with the stronger disapproval carried by cruel over unkind.
A word that contributes only expressive meaning can be removed from an utterance without altering its information content, though doing so tones down the forcefulness of the message.

Presupposed meaning arises from co-occurrence restrictions of two kinds: selectional restrictions, which follow from propositional meaning and are violated only in figurative language, and collocational restrictions, which are semantically arbitrary.
exception: selectional restrictions are deliberately violated in figurative language

statement: Because collocational restrictions are semantically arbitrary rather than derivable from propositional meaning, they tend to vary more across languages than selectional restrictions do, making them a frequent source of translation difficulty.
Evoked meaning arises from dialect variation (geographical, temporal, or social) and from register variation.

Register variation operates along three dimensions: field of discourse (what is going on), tenor of discourse (the relationships between participants), and mode of discourse (the role of the language and its medium of transmission).

Getting the tenor of discourse right in translation is difficult because it depends on whether a level of formality is judged appropriate from the source culture or the target culture, and the translator's choice depends on the perceived overall purpose of the translation.
condition: the decision depends on the perceived overall purpose of the translation

statement: A translator should ensure the translation matches the register expectations of its prospective receivers, unless the purpose of the translation is deliberately to give a flavour of the source culture.
exception: when the purpose is to give the target reader a flavour of the source culture

statement: Words have blurred, negotiable edges and their meaning is realized only in specific contexts, yet the translator must perceive word and utterance meaning very precisely in order to render it into another language.

There are no absolute guidelines for resolving non-equivalence; strategies can only be suggested for use in some contexts, because the choice of a suitable equivalent depends on linguistic and extra-linguistic factors and on how both the source writer and the translator manipulate the linguistic systems.
condition: the suitable equivalent depends on context and on both writers' handling of the linguistic systems

statement: A language's vocabulary can be viewed as a set of semantic fields (abstract conceptual divisions a community imposes on experience) subdivided into lexical sets; languages agree more on broad field headings and less as sub-fields become finely differentiated.

Languages tend to make only those distinctions in meaning that are relevant to their particular physical, historical, political, religious, cultural, economic, legal, technological, or social environment.

The semantic-field concept is limited: many words such as just, nevertheless, and only resist classification, so the notion works only for words with fairly well-defined propositional meaning, not for most words in a language.

Understanding how a semantic field is structured differently in the source and target languages lets a translator assess the value of a chosen item by seeing what alternatives it contrasts with, understanding not only what it is but what it is not.

Semantic fields are arranged hierarchically from superordinate (general word) to hyponym (specific word); the propositional meaning of a superordinate is necessarily part of the meaning of each of its hyponyms, but not the reverse.

A translator can exploit the superordinate/hyponym hierarchy to handle semantic gaps in the target language, often by modifying a superordinate or by circumlocutions built on modifying superordinates.
Semantic fields are not fixed; they change continually as new words and expressions enter the language and others are dropped when they become less relevant to the community's needs.

Non-equivalence at word level means the target language has no direct equivalent for a source word; the difficulty varies with the nature of the non-equivalence, and the context and purpose of the translation often rule out some strategies and favour others.
condition: context and purpose of the translation constrain which strategies apply

statement: It is neither possible nor helpful to relate specific types of non-equivalence to specific strategies in a fixed one-to-one mapping.

A common type of non-equivalence is the culture-specific concept: a source word expresses an abstract or concrete concept (a religious belief, social custom, or food) that is unknown in the target culture.
A source concept may be known in the target culture but not lexicalized, that is not allocated a single target-language word to express it.

A source word may be semantically complex even when morphologically simple: a single morpheme can express a set of meanings more complex than a whole sentence, because languages develop concise forms for concepts important enough to be discussed often.

Source and target languages may make different distinctions in meaning, so a distinction obligatory in one language may be unavailable in another, forcing the translator to recover the needed information from context.
condition: unless the context makes the intended distinction clear

statement: The target language may possess specific words (hyponyms) but lack a general word (superordinate) to head the relevant semantic field.
More commonly, the target language has the general word (superordinate) but lacks specific ones (hyponyms), since each language makes only the distinctions relevant to its environment.

Languages differ in physical or interpersonal perspective, such as the direction pairs come/go and take/bring or the interpersonal relationships they encode; for example Japanese has six equivalents of give depending on who gives to whom.

A target word may match the source word's propositional meaning but differ in expressive meaning; it is usually easier to add expressive meaning (with a modifier or adverb) than to subtract it, so the difference is hardest to handle when the target equivalent is more emotionally loaded than the source, as with sensitive religious, political, or sexual terms.

There may be no target equivalent for a particular source form such as a suffix or prefix; propositional meaning is relatively easy to paraphrase, but the expressive or evoked meaning carried by affixes is often lost or must be recovered elsewhere by compensatory techniques.

Even when a source form has a target equivalent, its frequency or purpose of use may differ; for instance English uses the continuous -ing form to bind clauses far more often than German or the Scandinavian languages, so rendering every -ing form identically produces stilted, unnatural style.

Loan words in the source text pose a special problem because they are often used for prestige or sophistication that is lost when the target has no equivalent loan word, and because false friends share a form across languages while conveying different meanings, even among unrelated languages.
Once a word is borrowed into a language, its subsequent development and the additional meanings it may take on cannot be predicted or controlled, which is why false friends arise.

When facing any non-equivalence a translator should first assess its significance in the given context, because not every instance matters; the aim is to convey the meaning of key words focal to the text, not to reproduce every aspect of every word in isolation.
condition: not every instance of non-equivalence is significant enough to reproduce

statement: Translation by a more general word (superordinate) is one of the commonest strategies for non-equivalence, especially in propositional meaning, and works across most languages because the hierarchical structure of semantic fields is not language-specific.

Translation by a more neutral or less expressive word is used when the nearest target equivalent carries the wrong expressive load; some of the lost expressive meaning can sometimes be restored by adding a modifier.

Translation by cultural substitution replaces a culture-specific item with a target item of different propositional meaning but similar impact; whether to use it depends on the licence given by the commissioner, the purpose of the translation, and the target community's tolerance for departing from propositional meaning.
condition: depends on commissioner licence, translation purpose, and target-community norms

statement: When an item is used chiefly for its expressive value, its literal or propositional meaning is not relevant in that context, which licenses a cultural substitute whose literal meaning differs but whose impact matches.
condition: when the source item functions mainly for expressive rather than propositional value

statement: Translation using a loan word or a loan word plus explanation is especially common for culture-specific items, modern concepts, and buzz words; giving the explanation once lets the loan word then stand alone without distracting the reader with repeated explanations.

Loan words are sometimes used in a translation not because the target lacks an equivalent but because they sound more modern, smart, or high-class, foregrounding evoked meaning over propositional meaning.

The freedom with which a translator may use loan words depends on the translation norms prevailing in the target society; for example Arabic and French are far less tolerant of loan words than Japanese.
condition: depends on the target society's translation norms

statement: Translation by paraphrase using a related word tends to be used when the source concept is lexicalized in the target language but in a different form, or when a form appears far more frequently in the source than would be natural in the target.

Translation by paraphrase using unrelated words is available when the source concept is not lexicalized at all in the target language; the paraphrase modifies a superordinate or unpacks the meaning of the source item, and is especially suited to semantically complex items.

Paraphrase achieves high precision in specifying propositional meaning but cannot convey expressive, evoked, or associative meaning, which attach only to stable lexical items with a history of recurrence, and it is cumbersome because it fills a one-item slot with several items.

Translation by omission is acceptable when an item's meaning is not vital to the development of the text and rendering it would require distracting explanation; because some loss is inevitable, omission should be used only as a last resort, when a smooth, readable translation clearly outweighs the value of the omitted meaning.
condition: only when the omitted item is not vital to the text and readability outweighs the lost meaning

statement: A translator may deliberately omit expressions that betray the source text's original point of view or audience orientation when the translation addresses a different audience.
condition: when the target text addresses a different audience than the source

statement: Translation by illustration is a useful option when a word lacking a target equivalent refers to a physical entity that can be pictured, particularly under space constraints where the text must stay short and concise.
condition: when the untranslatable item denotes a picturable physical entity

statement: The catalogued strategies for non-equivalence are not exhaustive; a translator should keep studying professional translations to discover further strategies and to learn to weigh each strategy's advantages and disadvantages in context.

Words rarely occur alone, and every language restricts how they combine: restrictions that admit no exceptions and apply to word classes are stated as grammatical rules, whereas restrictions that admit exceptions and apply to individual words cannot be stated as rules but recur as identifiable patterns of lexical patterning.

Lexical patterning above the word level falls under two headings, collocation and idioms and fixed expressions, and differences in this patterning between source and target languages are a major source of translation difficulty.

Collocation is the tendency of certain words to co-occur regularly in a language, and its patterns are largely arbitrary and independent of propositional meaning, both within a single language and across languages.
Synonyms and near-synonyms often have quite different sets of collocates, so one may be acceptable where the other is not even though their propositional meanings are close.

A collocation may hold across several grammatical forms of two words, or hold in some forms but not others, so a translator cannot assume that because two words collocate in one form they will collocate in all forms.

Differences in collocational patterning across languages can involve entirely different ways of portraying an event, not merely a different word paired with a given noun, as when Arabic focuses on the mother and English on the baby in describing childbirth.

Patterns of collocation reflect a language community's preferences for particular modes of expression rather than any inherent order in the world, though some collocations do directly reflect the material, social, or moral environment in which they occur.
Every word has a collocational range, the set of collocates typically associated with it; some words have a much broader range than others.

Two factors influence a word's collocational range: its level of specificity, since a more general word has a broader range than its hyponyms, and the number of senses it has, since each sense tends to attract a different set of collocates.

Unlike grammatical statements, statements about collocation concern what is typical or untypical rather than admissible or inadmissible, so there is no such thing as an impossible collocation and collocational ranges are not fixed but grow as words attract new collocates through analogy or deliberate creation.

In wording a message a writer can either reinforce existing collocations or vary them, for instance by extending a range through analogy; a marked collocation is an unusual combination that challenges the reader's expectations and is used in fiction, poetry, humour, and advertising to create images and catch attention.

Collocational markedness is not an absolute quality; it always depends on the norm in a given register, so a collocation that is marked in everyday language may be common and unmarked within a specialized register.

Register-specific collocations extend far beyond a discipline's terminology, so translating specialized texts requires knowing which collocates are compatible with a term in both languages; being a native speaker does not guarantee the ability to assess register-specific collocational acceptability, which is why translation training includes specialized-language courses.

A word's meaning often depends on its collocational pattern rather than being possessed in isolation, so taking account of collocational meaning instead of substituting individual dictionary equivalents is crucial at the first, interpretation stage of translation.

When a translation is criticized as inaccurate or inappropriate, the fault may be the translator's failure to recognize a collocational pattern whose meaning differs from the sum of the meanings of its individual elements.

Even when collocational patterns in two languages appear to match closely in form, they may not carry the same meaning, as run a car means own and maintain a car in English but drive it fast in modern Greek.

The engrossing effect of source-text patterning can lead a translator to produce odd target collocations for no good reason; a good countermeasure is to set the draft aside for a few hours and return to respond to it as a target reader would, and translators should avoid carrying over source collocational patterns untypical of the target language unless there is a very good reason.
exception: unless there is a very good reason to keep the source pattern

statement: A translator can misinterpret a source collocation through interference from the native language when the source collocation corresponds in form to a common target collocation, which is one reason professional translators normally work from a foreign language into their native language or language of habitual use.

Rendering an unmarked source collocation involves a tension between typicality and accuracy: the ideal target collocation is both natural and meaning-preserving, but this cannot always be achieved, and whether the resulting change in meaning is acceptable depends on how significant that change is in the given context.
condition: the acceptability of the meaning change depends on its significance in context

statement: Some loss, addition, or skewing of meaning is often unavoidable because language systems are too different to produce exact replicas, and using established, familiar target patterns keeps the communication channels open and distinguishes a smooth translation that reads like an original from a clumsy one that sounds foreign.

Culture-specific collocations convey associations of ideas unfamiliar to the target reader and point to concepts not easily accessible, so translating them involves an unavoidable partial increase in information, because unfamiliar associations cannot be introduced without hinting to the reader how to interpret them.

Ideally a marked collocation in the source text is rendered by a similarly marked collocation in the target language, but this is always subject to the constraints of the target language and to the purpose of the translation.
condition: subject to target-language constraints and the purpose of the translation

statement: A translator should not feel obliged to reproduce every aspect of the source text regardless of its significance in the target context, because reproducing source collocations that carry no significance for the target reader communicates very little to them.

Language is not a set of words usable together in free variation: words have a certain tolerance of compatibility, and collocational patterns themselves carry meaning and can be culture-specific, which together with their arbitrary nature gives rise to numerous translation pitfalls.

Idioms and fixed expressions lie at the opposite extreme from collocations in flexibility of form and transparency of meaning: they are frozen patterns that allow little or no variation, and idioms often carry meanings that cannot be deduced from their individual components.

Under normal circumstances an idiom allows no variation: a speaker cannot change the order of its words, delete a word, add a word, replace a word with another, or change its grammatical structure, unless deliberately making a joke or a play on words.
exception: when the speaker is consciously making a joke or a play on words

statement: Fixed expressions and proverbs allow little variation like idioms but usually have transparent meanings; nonetheless a fixed expression means more than the sum of its words and must be taken as a unit, and it evokes the stereotyped contexts of its use, performing a stabilizing function in communication.

Because active competence in using a foreign language's idioms and fixed expressions rarely matches a native speaker's, translators should work only into their language of habitual use or mother tongue.
exception: in exceptional cases a second language of native knowledge

statement: Idioms and fixed expressions pose two main problems in translation: recognizing and interpreting the idiom correctly, and rendering the various aspects of its meaning into the target language; both difficulties are much more pronounced for idioms than for fixed expressions.

The first difficulty with an idiom is recognizing it; easily recognizable idioms violate truth conditions, are grammatically ill-formed, or begin with like, and generally the less sense an expression makes literally in context, the more likely it is an idiom, so an opaque expression can be a blessing that alerts the translator to an idiom's presence.

An idiom is easily misinterpreted in two cases: misleading idioms that offer a plausible literal reading alongside their idiomatic meaning, tempting an unfamiliar translator to miss the idiom, and source idioms whose target look-alike has a totally or partially different meaning, tempting the translator to impose the target interpretation.

A translator should examine the collocational environment of any expression whose meaning is not readily accessible, because idioms have their own collocational patterns and enter lexical sets different from those of their component words, so knowledge of collocation helps recognize an idiom even when it does not reveal its meaning.

An idiom or fixed expression may have no equivalent in the target language, since how a language expresses a meaning is unpredictable and only occasionally matches another; however, containing culture-specific items does not by itself make an idiom untranslatable, because it is the meaning and its cultural associations, not the specific items, that determine translatability.
An idiom may have a similar counterpart in the target language whose context of use differs, so that the two carry different connotations or are not pragmatically transferable.
When an idiom is used in both its literal and idiomatic senses at once, the play on idiom can be reproduced only if the target-language idiom corresponds to the source idiom in both form and meaning.
condition: only when a target idiom matches the source in both form and meaning

statement: The convention of using idioms, the contexts in which they are acceptable, and their frequency of use differ across languages; English uses idioms widely in advertising and the tabloid press but sparingly in quality-press news, whereas languages such as Arabic and Chinese that associate the written mode with formality tend to avoid idioms in written texts.

How to translate an idiom depends on more than whether a similar-meaning target idiom exists: the significance of its specific lexical items (whether they are manipulated elsewhere) and the appropriateness of idiomatic language in the target register also matter, so a strategy's acceptability always depends on context.
condition: the acceptability of a strategy depends on the context of the specific idiom

statement: Finding a target idiom of similar meaning and form is not always the ideal solution; questions of style, register, and rhetorical effect must be weighed, and translators should resist the strong unconscious urge to search for a receptor-language idiom however inappropriate it may be.
The strategy of using a target idiom of similar meaning and similar form conveys roughly the same meaning with equivalent lexical items, but this kind of match can only occasionally be achieved.
The strategy of using an idiom of similar meaning but dissimilar form renders a source idiom with a target idiom that conveys a similar meaning while consisting of different lexical items.

Translation by paraphrase is by far the most common way of translating an idiom when no match exists in the target language or when using idiomatic language would be stylistically inappropriate in the target text.
condition: when no target idiom matches or idiomatic language is stylistically inappropriate in the target

statement: An idiom may be omitted altogether in the target text when it has no close match, its meaning cannot be easily paraphrased, or for stylistic reasons.

Compensation lets a translator omit or play down a feature such as idiomaticity where it occurs in the source text and reintroduce it elsewhere in the target text; it can make up for any loss of meaning, emotional force, or stylistic effect that cannot be reproduced directly at a given point.

Using the typical phraseology of the target language, its natural collocations, its own fixed and semi-fixed expressions, and the right level of idiomaticity, greatly enhances a translation's readability and, other factors being equal, can make it pass for an original.

The lexical resources of a language, its stock of words and expressions and its established patterns of collocation, provide ready-made ways of analysing and reporting experience and largely determine both what can be said and how it can be said.

The grammatical system is a powerful factor determining which distinctions a language regularly makes in reporting experience, such as time, number, gender, shape, visibility, person, proximity, and animacy; there is no uniform or objective way of reporting events, and each language preselects certain areas as fundamental.

Grammar is the set of rules that determine how words and phrases combine and what information must be made regularly explicit; a language can express any information its speakers need, but its grammatical system determines the ease with which notions such as time reference or gender can be made explicit.

The notional categories once assumed basic and universal, such as time, number, and gender, are not in fact universal; languages differ widely in the range of notions they choose to make explicit on a regular basis.

Grammar is organized along two dimensions: morphology, the way a word's form changes to indicate grammatical contrasts and which determines the basic information that must be expressed, and syntax, the allowed linear sequences of word classes and functional elements, which restricts how messages may be organized.

The most important difference for translation is that grammatical choices, drawn from closed systems, are largely obligatory and rule out other choices from the same system by default, whereas lexical choices, drawn from open-ended sets, are largely optional.

Grammatical structure is far more resistant to change and to speaker manipulation than lexical structure, deviant grammar being accepted only in restricted contexts such as poetry, advertisements, and jokes, so in translation grammar often acts as a straitjacket that forces the translator along a course that may not follow the source text as closely as desired.
exception: in restricted contexts such as poetry, advertising, and jokes where grammar may be flouted for effect

statement: Languages are differently equipped to express real-world relations and do not express all aspects of meaning with equal ease; it is difficult to find a notional category that is regularly and uniformly expressed in all languages.

Differences in the grammatical structures of source and target languages often change the information content of the message: information may have to be added when the target has a grammatical category the source lacks, or omitted when the target lacks a category the source has.
Details that are ignored in the source text but must be specified in the target language pose a serious dilemma for the translator when they cannot be reasonably inferred from the context.
condition: when the obligatory target detail cannot be inferred from context

statement: When the target language lacks a grammatical category the source expresses, rendering all the conceptual information is difficult in practice: the associated information is optional and low-frequency, so specifying it repeatedly sounds unnatural, and expressing it lexically gives it more weight in the target text than it carried in the source.

Countability is probably universal and expressed lexically in all languages, but not all languages have a grammatical category of number, and those that do do not view it identically, distinguishing for example singular and plural in English, a dual in Arabic and Eskimo, or a trial in Fijian.
A translator moving from a language that has number distinctions into one with no category of number has two main options: omit the information on number, or encode it lexically.

Number or duality can be encoded lexically where important, but a translator working into a language without a number category must not overspecify: repeatedly stating information the target normally leaves unspecified makes the translation awkward and unnatural unless the context demands it.
exception: unless the context specifically demands the number information

statement: Gender is a grammatical distinction classifying a noun or pronoun as masculine or feminine, applying to nouns for animate beings and inanimate objects alike, with determiners, adjectives, and sometimes verbs agreeing with the noun in gender.

English has no grammatical category of gender but expresses gender in some semantic areas and in the third-person-singular pronoun system; languages differ widely in how far gender extends, from French plural ils/elles to Arabic gender in second- and third-person pronouns and verb forms to none in Chinese and Indonesian.

In most languages with a gender category the masculine is the dominant or unmarked term, so using a feminine form conveys more specific information because it rules out masculine reference, whereas the masculine form does not rule out feminine reference.

A gender-neutral or feminine-as-unmarked ideological stance is easy to adopt in English because it affects only items like he, but is hard to transfer into a language where gender pervades noun, pronoun, verb, and adjective concord, such as Arabic, without sacrificing the readability of the target text.

Gender distinctions matter more in translation when the referent is human: the gender of inanimate or animal referents is largely arbitrary and adjusting it is straightforward, whereas the pronominal function of gender for human referents reflects a genuine, non-arbitrary distinction that speakers universally recognize.

When neither the unmarked masculine nor the feminine form fits, such as a product used predominantly by women where the masculine would be marked but the feminine might exclude male users, a translator can avoid specifying gender by restructuring, for example using the passive voice to omit the verb's subject.
condition: when both marked and unmarked gender forms are inappropriate in the context

statement: The category of person defines participant roles through a closed pronoun system, most commonly first, second, and third person, and may additionally encode number, gender, social status, intimacy, inclusive/exclusive, and familiar/non-familiar dimensions, with systems varying in richness across languages.

Many modern European languages, though not English, have a formality/politeness dimension in the person system in which a non-second-singular pronoun (usually second- or third-person plural, such as vous, Sie, usted) is used with a singular addressee to express deference or non-familiarity.

Translating pronouns from English into a formality-marking language forces decisions along dimensions such as gender, intimacy, and inclusive/exclusive reference that are not explicit in English and not always recoverable from context, while translating into English frequently loses that information, and encoding it fully in English is usually too cumbersome.

Translating into a language that marks formality or gender in pronouns forces the translator to make conscious decisions about the relationships and social standing of the characters, because the grammatical system compels choices that shape how events and relationships are presented.

The familiar/non-familiar dimension of the pronoun system reflects the tenor of discourse and conveys subtle meaning, but it varies significantly across social groups and changes over time with social values, making it among the most problematic aspects of grammar in translation.

Tense and aspect are grammatical categories in many languages, the verb encoding time relations (past, present, future) and aspectual differences (completion, continuation, momentariness); systems vary widely in fineness, and languages such as Chinese, Malay, and Yurok have no formal tense or aspect, indicating time only optionally through particles and adverbials while relying more heavily on context.

Tense and aspect do not always serve time reference: in some languages such as Hopi the tense system mainly signals modal meanings, and tense/aspect can carry subtle discourse meanings, as with the present-for-indicative and past-for-informative correlation that distinguishes what an academic paper states from what its research did.

Even when two languages have similar basic tense systems, their tense-based signalling systems can differ, so a translator must not mechanically map each source tense onto a matching target tense but must bear in mind the additional meanings the target forms can carry, as the Japanese non-past can express personal judgement.
Imposing a textbook rule of consistent tense and aspect use across a text can destroy the natural signalling system of the target language.

Voice is a grammatical category defining the relationship between a verb and its subject: in active clauses the subject is the agent performing the action, and in passive clauses the subject is the affected entity while the agent may or may not be specified.

The agentless passive is far more frequent than the agent-specified passive, because the main function of the passive in most languages is to construct agentless clauses, and most languages have varied mechanisms such as dummy subjects and reflexives for the same purpose.

Languages with a voice category use the passive with different frequency (German, Russian, and French use it less than English, favouring reflexives), and this frequency usually reflects a stylistic choice or convention; scientific and technical English relies heavily on the passive to project objectivity and distance the writer, a norm so entrenched that writers find it hard to break away.

The passive does not serve the same function in all languages: in Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese, and Thai its main function is to express adversity, so a passive structure can carry connotations of unpleasantness even when the event depicted is neutral.

Mechanically rendering a passive by a passive and an active by an active can distort a translation by changing the information, the linear arrangement of agent and affected entity, and the focus of the message; the translator must weigh this against producing a smooth, natural target text, because it is always the function of a grammatical category, not its form, that is paramount in translation.

The key considerations for voice are the frequency of active, passive, and similar structures in the source and target languages, their stylistic value in different text types, and above all the function the passive serves in each language.

Modality, the speaker's attitude of certainty, possibility, or obligation, is expressed in quite different forms across languages, so a literal rendering of a modal form often misses the modal meaning and the translator should render the function instead, as a Hebrew question about possibility functions as a command.

Other grammatical categories such as mood, direct and indirect speech, and causativity also pose translation difficulties, and translators should investigate and compare how these categories and their associated meanings are expressed in their source and target languages.

Languages vary in how much they rely on word order to signal relationships between clause elements: English and Chinese have relatively fixed word order so meaning often depends entirely on element order, whereas languages with elaborate case inflections such as Russian have freer word order, making order a stylistic resource for emphasis and contrast.
Word order is extremely important in translation because it plays a major role in maintaining a coherent point of view and in orienting messages at the level of the whole text.

Lexical items and grammatical structures carry only a meaning potential that is realized in communicative events, so text, defined as the verbal record of a communicative event, is an instance of language in use rather than language as an abstract system.
Bad translations are among the closest things to non-text in real life, so a translator must view the text as a whole both at the beginning and at the end of the translation process.
A good translator does not begin to translate until having read the text at least once and grasped the gist of its overall message.

Producing a target version acceptable as a text in its own right requires that its phraseology and collocational and grammatical patterning conform to target-language norms; even then it may still sound foreign or fail to make sense, because acceptable collocations and grammar enhance individual sentences but do not by themselves make sentences and paragraphs add up to a coherent text.

Features of text organization are language- and culture-specific, since each linguistic community has preferred ways of organizing its types of discourse, which is why target readers can identify a lexically and grammatically normal text as a translation or as foreign.

In most cases the translator's ultimate aim is a measure of equivalence at text level rather than at word or phrase level, wanting the reader to accept the translation as a text in its own right by adjusting source-text organization to the target language's preferred discourse patterns.
exception: in some contexts, such as biblical or koranic translation, equivalence at the word or phrase level takes priority

statement: Text organization is less well defined than lexis and grammar, because it is far more straightforward to decide what constitutes an acceptable sentence than an acceptable sentence sequence, paragraph, or discourse, and text studies remain a relatively recent development with little describing non-English discourse conventions.

The connections that make a stretch of language a text are of several kinds: thematic and information structures that develop and maintain the topic, cohesion that establishes surface interrelations among persons and events, and coherence and implicature that supply the underlying semantic connections.

Genre and text type describe how textual material is packaged along patterns familiar to the reader, classified either by institutional context (journal article, newspaper editorial) or by rhetorical mode (narration, exposition, argumentation, instruction), and both classifications help define translation problems and justify strategies.

A translator should be aware not only of cognitive meaning and syntax but also of a text's information dynamics; this awareness need not require formal theme-rheme analysis and may rely on intuition, but theory should not be avoided where it helps define problems.

Word order functions as a textual strategy that controls information flow, not merely as a grammatical feature, so of the many formulations available for a message a writer normally chooses the one that makes the flow of information clearer in the given context.

Information flows more smoothly when a sentence starts from an element already established in preceding discourse before presenting new information, keeping the progression of links between sentences clean and easy to follow.

A translator should treat a clause as a message with an interactional organization reflecting the addresser-addressee relationship, not merely as a string of grammatical and lexical elements, because it is this interactional organization that drives choices maintaining a clear progression of links and a coherent point of view across the text.

The clause as a message is analysed through thematic structure and information structure, and there are two competing approaches, the Hallidayan separating approach that treats them as distinct and the Prague School combining approach that conflates them; since the two can analyse the same clause differently, a translator should use whichever explanation fits the languages of interest and ignore the rest.

In thematic structure a clause divides into a theme, what the clause is about, placed in initial position and orienting back to prior discourse while departing forward, and a rheme, what is said about the theme, which carries the information the speaker most wants to convey; every clause thus has the structure of a message that says something about something.

Thematic analysis is hierarchical, since a multi-clause sentence has layered theme-rheme structures, and conjunctions and disjuncts, though inherently thematic and clause-initial, are not part of the propositional content and so are not thematic in the same way as the main clause elements subject, predicator, object, complement, and adjunct.

In the Hallidayan model theme and rheme correlate highly with subject and predicate except in marked themes, but the theme-rheme distinction is text-based, so its value lies not in explaining individual sentence structure but in illuminating what controls information flow across a text.
exception: the correlation does not hold for marked themes

statement: Theme and rheme account for the acceptability of a sequence in context rather than its grammaticality, so a text can be perfectly grammatical clause by clause yet thematically ill-formed, feeling disjointed and lacking orientation.

Poor translations often show thematic ill-formedness in which themes fail to link to previous themes or rhemes and each sentence stands in a vacuum, so a translator must take account of thematic structure and maintain a coherent point of view.

The selection of an individual clause's theme is not in itself significant, but the overall choice and ordering of themes, especially those of independent clauses, plays an important part in organizing a text and providing a point of orientation.

Different text types favour particular themes, so English travel brochures and guidebooks thematize place adjuncts to use location as a point of orientation while narrative texts thematize temporal adjuncts.

A series of homogeneous themes, such as a repeated first-person I, provides a point of orientation and a method of development that maintains continuity and a coherent point of view across a stretch of text.

A thematic pattern natural in one language may not transfer to another, so an ego-centred series of I themes natural in English must be replaced in Arabic by a process-centred pattern of thematized inflected verbs, and Halliday's model may be less workable for verb-initial languages.

At the thematic level a translator faces three possibilities: preserve the original thematic patterning when its elements sit naturally in theme position in the target, or abandon it when preserving it would distort the target while ensuring the target has its own method of development and continuity, or switch to the Prague model when Halliday's model does not apply to the language.

A translator must not underestimate the cumulative effect of thematic choices on interpretation: when the themes of a paragraph's sentences share a semantic field that field is perceived as the paragraph's method of development, so whatever is placed in initial position in the target must add up to a discernible method of development and orientation.

Meaning, choice, and markedness are interrelated: a linguistic element carries meaning to the extent that it is selected, so the more obligatory an element's position the less marked and weaker its meaning, and the less expected a choice the more marked and the more meaning it carries, so the more marked a choice the greater the need for it to be motivated.

Placing an element in theme position is not automatically a marked choice; markedness depends on how frequently the element occurs in theme position and how mobile it is in the clause, so each clause type has one unmarked thematic structure, which in English signals the mood of the clause (subject in declaratives, the wh-word or auxiliary in interrogatives, the verb in imperatives).

A marked theme foregrounds a particular element as the clause's topic and point of departure, giving it local prominence at clause level, whereas rheme position gives an element prominence at the overall discourse level.
English has three main types of marked theme: fronted theme, predicated theme, and identifying theme.

Fronting moves into initial position an item otherwise unusual there; fronting adjuncts is only mildly marked because adverbials are mobile, whereas fronting objects or complements is much more marked and foregrounds expressive meaning or contrast rather than a method of development, and fronting the predicator is the most marked of all, with the same structure carrying different markedness across languages.

Using the passive voice lets a speaker select as theme what would have been the object of an active clause without making it marked, whereas fronting the object foregrounds it and gives it local prominence, so passive and fronting are distinct thematic tools.

When translating a structure whose markedness differs across languages, match the function rather than the form: an unmarked Arabic predicator-subject order should become an unmarked English subject-predicator order rather than a highly marked English fronted predicator, and an emphatic English fronted predicator should be conveyed into Arabic by a target emphasis device such as the particle qad.

Predicated theme uses an it- or cleft structure to place an element near the clause's start as its theme (the theme being the element after the verb to be, not It); it foregrounds that element, lets the subject act as a marked theme, often implies contrast, and signals information structure by presenting the element after It plus BE as the new, important item.

Identifying theme uses a wh- or pseudo-cleft structure to place an element in theme by nominalization; both predicated and identifying themes often imply contrast, but a predicated theme presents its thematic element as new information whereas an identifying theme presents its thematic element as known information.

Predicated and identifying themes are marked but fairly common in English because they overcome word-order restrictions and signal given versus new information independently of intonation, and since stress is unavailable in written English they are more common in written than in spoken English.

Predicated and identifying themes must be handled carefully in translation because they are far more marked in relatively free-word-order languages such as German, so an experienced translator replaces most of them with less marked target structures such as simple fronting.

A translator should learn to use the thematization devices available in each language rather than only be aware of markedness levels, since for example fronted information in a Dutch clause lends itself to an English it-cleft, and pitfalls of underusing such devices worsen when translating into the non-native language.

Languages with relatively free word order such as German can thematize clause elements simply by fronting them, so they rarely need the intricate cleft structures that relatively fixed-word-order languages resort to for thematization.

Normalizing a marked source structure into an unmarked target structure is not always the best strategy, because a different but similarly marked target structure, such as the Arabic particle inna, can preserve the prominence the writer gave an element while still sounding natural.

The Hallidayan view that theme is whatever comes in initial position is simple to apply but has drawbacks: partial circularity, and a failure to relate fixed-word-order SVO languages to free-word-order languages where the verb is often initial, so it does not address that some languages regularly thematize participants while others thematize processes.

In topic-prominent languages such as Chinese, Japanese, and Korean the topic always occurs in initial position and coincides with theme, but topic differs from theme in that it is always definite, its scope extends beyond the clause, it controls anaphoric reference so later clauses can drop the subject, and its function is to set the framework of time, location, or reference within which the sentence holds.

A Chinese-style topic has no fully adequate English packaging device, so translating it with an expression such as as for is often incorrect because the English phrase implies a contrastiveness that the Chinese topic need not carry, and because topic-comment structures are the norm in topic-prominent languages but marked and infrequent in English, learners and translators into English tend to overuse them.

Information structure divides a message into given and new and is hearer-oriented, unlike the speaker-oriented theme-rheme distinction: given information is the common ground already known to the hearer and provides a reference point, while new information is what the speaker wishes to convey.

Information structure, like thematic structure, is a feature of context rather than of the language system, so which part of a message is given and which is new can only be decided within a linguistic or situational context, and the same message segments differently in response to different questions.
The normal, unmarked order places given information before new information, which has been found to aid comprehension and recall and is explicitly recommended to writers.

The given-before-new principle underlies both end-focus, the tendency to present information from low to high information value, and end-weight, the tendency to place longer and heavier structures toward the end of the clause, and similar principles operate in languages such as German and Brazilian Portuguese.

Problems arise in translation when a principle such as end-weight clashes with a basic grammatical principle of the target language, such as subject-before-predicate in English, since adhering to subject-before-predicate while ignoring end-weight yields an awkward heavy-subject, light-verb result; the clash can be resolved, for example by switching from passive to active and inserting a subject such as This paper.

In spoken English each information unit is realized as a tone group whose tonic accent, perceived as stress, falls on the new element and carries the information focus, the device English speakers use to highlight the core of a message.

The boundaries of given and new elements cannot be decided on phonological evidence alone, because the tonic accent normally falls on the last item without marking where the given element ends and the new begins, so one must look at the surrounding context to establish the boundary.

Given and new information can be analysed in written as well as spoken language, because context establishes whether information was introduced earlier and many signalling devices are shared: definiteness generally marks given information and indefiniteness new information, and given information tends to be grammatically subordinate while new information appears in the predicate.

Because stress is unavailable in written language, syntactic devices such as cleft and pseudo-cleft structures signal information status, with the item in theme position presented as new and the item in rheme position presented as given.

Failure to appreciate how specific syntactic structures signal given and new information can cause unnecessary shifts in translation that distort the original's information structure, such as rendering a cleft so that an element meant as new is presented as given; the shift can be avoided by using a natural target structure, such as a pseudo-cleft, that preserves the given and new status of the elements.

Punctuation signals information structure in written language, for example distinguishing a defining relative clause, which identifies its antecedent and adds no new information, from a comma-marked non-defining relative clause, which presents new information.

Different languages use different devices to signal information structure, so a translator must develop sensitivity to each language's signalling system; the attenuation theory that given information is conveyed in a weaker form (lower pitch, pronominalization) fits English and many languages but not all, since pronominalization is rare in Japanese and Chinese, French, Finnish, and Arabic rely on word order, case, or definiteness instead.

Chinese signals definiteness, and hence givenness, largely by word order, since nominals occurring before the main verb tend to be definite while those occurring after the main verb may be either definite or indefinite.

Most commonly a given element is one recoverable because it has been mentioned before, but information may also be treated as given because it is predictable or contextually salient; the key notion is consciousness, given information being what the speaker assumes is already in the addressee's consciousness and new information being what the speaker introduces into it.

How long a previously mentioned element stays in the addressee's consciousness before it must be reintroduced as new depends on the number of intervening sentences without mention and on discourse boundaries such as a change of scene, which matters for abridging, expanding, or rewriting; after enough intervening text and a marked scene change, an item is properly reintroduced as new, for instance with an indefinite noun group.
condition: depends on intervening distance and whether a discourse boundary such as a scene change intervenes

statement: Givenness is assigned by the speaker and need not correlate with the reality of the situation: a speaker may present an element as given without warrant, a common political ploy because presenting information as given implies it is established, agreed, and non-negotiable, or may present a previously mentioned element as new for contrast or surprise.

Information structure, unlike English thematic structure, is realized chiefly by tonicity rather than element sequence: in unmarked structure the information focus falls on the whole rheme or part of it, and the speaker can shift the focus onto other elements, such as the theme or the verb, to convey surprise, contrast, or emphasis on the truth of the utterance.

In written language marked information structure is signalled through typography or punctuation such as italics, and a focal element may be new in the sense of being contrastive rather than previously unmentioned.

A language that does not use phonological stress, such as French, conveys what English signals by intonation through lexical means such as adding an emphatic phrase or through labelling a repetition as a repetition.

A rheme can be marked by stripping away the clause's theme to foreground the rheme as the core of the message; marked theme gives prominence to an element as linking information, whereas marked rheme gives prominence to an element as the core of the message.

Themeless clauses are a fairly common and effective English stylistic device that foregrounds the rheme and can create a surprise effect, but some languages such as French require a subject with every verb and cannot reproduce them, forcing the translator to spell out the interpretation and lose the surprise or to use a compensating device such as repetition plus temporal signalling in Arabic.

Theme often coincides with given and rheme with new, because unmarked information structure places given before new and unmarked thematic structure places theme before rheme, which is why Prague linguists build givenness into the definition of theme and newness into the definition of rheme.

Functional Sentence Perspective is a Prague School alternative to the Hallidayan account in which the communicative goals of an interaction cause a clause's fixed syntactic structure to function in different perspectives, and a translator should become familiar with at least one FSP model because it can better explain the interactional organization of free-word-order languages and underlies much translation-problem analysis.

Communicative dynamism is the extent to which a linguistic element pushes the communication forward, so foundation-laying, context-dependent elements carry a low degree of dynamism and are thematic while core-constituting, context-independent elements carry a higher degree and form the non-theme.

Firbas's notion of context-dependence is narrower than Halliday's given/new: it is purely linguistic, treating any information not present in the immediately relevant verbal or situational context as context-independent, and does not extend to the psychological consciousness aspect that Halliday's given/new distinction covers.

In FSP the non-theme divides into a transition, consisting of the elements that link the foundation-laying and core-constituting parts of the clause (chiefly the temporal and modal exponents of the verb and link verbs, carrying the lowest dynamism within the non-theme), and the rheme, the core of the message carrying the highest dynamism.

Unlike the Hallidayan model where the verb is generally part of the rheme, FSP assigns the verb thematic or rhematic status by context and semantics, so the less notional content a verb carries the more naturally it goes with the theme, and a verb whose content has already been mentioned is thematic.

In FSP communicative dynamism results from the interplay of three factors, linear modification (position and syntax), semantic structure, and context, where semantic structure and context are hierarchically superior to position, so a pronoun or a definite expression is thematic regardless of where it stands in the clause except when presented contrastively.
exception: except when the element is presented contrastively

statement: Because FSP does not treat position as the sole criterion for thematic status, two orderings of the same message can share one thematic analysis, so FSP has no marked theme defined by initial position; instead it explains a marked structure as a reversed rheme-theme (pathetic) order that adds an emotional or contrastive layer, and both the Hallidayan and Prague accounts recognize such a sequence as marked.

Word-order patterns fulfil syntactic, semantic, and communicative functions at once, and languages give these different priorities depending on how fixed their word order is; English gives the syntactic principle the leading role, so free-word-order languages such as Czech follow communicative sentence perspective more faithfully than English does.

Fixed-word-order languages show greater tension between syntax and communicative function than free-word-order languages, so translating between languages with different priorities and syntactic restrictions necessarily involves some skewing of information flow.

Voice change resolves tension between syntax and communicative function by changing the verb's voice to reorder clause elements, but when substituting active for passive the supplied subject must preserve the impersonality normally associated with the passive, such as choosing This paper as subject.
condition: the supplied active subject must preserve the impersonality of the passive

statement: Change of verb replaces a verb with a similar-meaning one usable in a different syntactic configuration, such as give and get or buy-from and sell-to, to reorder elements without significant meaning change, but many such pairs are equivalent only in theory because each language's own phraseology makes one option unnatural.

Nominalization replaces a verbal form with a nominal one followed by a semantically empty verb or a weak subject, letting a translator preserve a verb-initial source's thematic organization while obeying an obligatory subject-verb order in the target; it is a viable but under-used strategy, well suited to thematizing processes when reporting research.

Extraposition changes the position of an entire clause, for instance through cleft and pseudo-cleft structures, providing an escape to a higher and freer level when word order is relatively fixed at clause level.

In practice the dislocation-resolving strategies are rarely used, the most common approach by far being to abandon the source text's thematic organization in favour of the target language's word-order principles, which often yields a perfectly acceptable target text, so a translator need not follow the source's thematic organization of every clause though awareness of information flow and of these strategies remains important.

A translator cannot always follow the original's thematic organization and should present the target text from a similar perspective when possible, but restrictions on word order, the end-weight principle, and the target's natural phraseology often force abandoning it; what matters is that the target text has its own thematic organization, reads naturally, does not distort the original's information structure, preserves any special emphasis of marked structures where possible, and maintains a coherent point of view in its own right.

Each language has its own patterns for conveying the interrelationships of persons and events, and these patterns may not be ignored in any language if the translation is to be understood by its readers.

Cohesion is the network of lexical, grammatical, and other relations that link parts of a text and require the reader to interpret words and expressions by reference to others in the surrounding sentences; it is a surface relation connecting the actual words and expressions, in contrast to coherence.
Halliday and Hasan identify five main cohesive devices in English: reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical cohesion.

In the Halliday and Hasan cohesion model, reference is textual rather than semantic: it is the relationship of identity between two linguistic expressions, where the reader retrieves the identity of what is discussed by referring to another expression in the context, and the cohesion lies in the continuity of reference.

Every language has reference items, most commonly pronouns and also words like the, this, and those in English, that direct the reader elsewhere for their interpretation and thereby let the reader trace participants, entities, and events through a text.

A common English pattern for building reference chains is to mention a participant explicitly first, by name or title, then use a pronoun to refer back; languages with number and gender distinctions in their pronoun system are less constrained in using this device because different pronouns reduce the chance of confusing reference.

Reference may also be situational, with a pronoun pointing to an entity present in the context of situation rather than in the text, and co-reference across different descriptions of the same entity depends on world knowledge rather than textual competence; for translation it is difficult and unhelpful to draw a firm line between textual and extralinguistic reference.
Cohesive elements for referring back to an already-mentioned entity form a continuum from full repetition through synonym, superordinate, and general word to pronominal reference at the other end.

Patterns of reference, or anaphora, vary considerably both within and across languages, with text type an important factor within a language, so each language has general preferences for certain reference patterns as well as specific preferences sensitive to text type.

Languages differ in preferred reference devices: English relies heavily on pronominal reference to trace participants, Hebrew and Brazilian Portuguese favour proper names and lexical repetition, and Japanese and Chinese rarely use pronouns, signalling continuity by omitting the subjects of following clauses so the reader supplies the last-mentioned or inferable participant.

When source and target languages favour different reference patterns, the translator must rework reference to the target's norms, for example turning a subject-omitting Japanese chain into an English-typical name-then-pronoun chain through rewordings and omissions rather than reproducing inferable chains.

Substitution and ellipsis are grammatical rather than semantic relations: substitution replaces an item with another such as do, one, or the same, while ellipsis omits an item entirely but only where the grammatical structure itself points to the item that fills the slot, and the details are highly language-specific.

The boundaries between reference, substitution, and ellipsis are not clear-cut, and the technical distinctions need not concern the translator; what matters is that every language has its own devices for creating texture and that a text hangs together by virtue of the semantic and structural relationships among its elements.

Except when carrying out a linguistic exercise, a translator should not transfer the source text's cohesive devices into the target text but should rework the methods of establishing links to suit the target language's textual norms, because each language's grammar encourages certain devices and each genre's norms suggest or rule out options.
exception: unless carrying out a linguistic exercise such as for research

statement: A language's grammatical resources shape its choice of cohesive device: Arabic verb-subject agreement in gender and number plus pronominal suffixes make pronominal reference safe across embedded clauses, whereas English, with few such distinctions, favours lexical repetition to avoid ambiguity, and in legal and semi-legal texts lexical repetition is the norm even where a pronoun would be unambiguous.

Conjunction uses formal markers to relate sentences, clauses, and paragraphs; unlike reference, substitution, and ellipsis it does not ask the reader to supply missing information but signals how to relate what is about to be said to what came before, expressing a small set of general relations: additive, adversative, causal, temporal, and continuative.

The same conjunction may signal different relations depending on context, these relations can be expressed by other means such as verbs like follow or cause and are often recognized even without an explicit signal, and conjunctive relations may reflect relations internal to the unfolding text, such as first, second, and third marking stages, not only relations between external phenomena.

Languages vary greatly in the types and frequency of conjunctions they prefer, and because conjunction signals relations between chunks of information it is bound up with how information is chunked and how the relations between chunks are perceived and signalled, giving insight into the whole logic of the discourse.

English and Arabic contrast sharply in conjunction: English presents information in small chunks with a wide variety of conjunctions and a developed punctuation system, whereas Arabic groups information into very large chunks and uses few conjunctions such as wa and fa, each with a wide context-dependent range, relying heavily on reader inference, so short sentences, varied conjunctions, and the absence of typical Arabic conjunctions mark a text as translated rather than original Arabic.

Typical target-language conjunctions may be added to a translation to make it smoother even when the source uses none, but because typical Arabic conjunctions are semantically more general, a translator must choose between a smooth text with less precise conjunctions and a precise one with a varied array, and in practice most translators strike a balance between the two.

At the level of cohesion, using a typical target conjunction enhances naturalness sometimes at the expense of accuracy, while directly paraphrasing a source conjunction that has no established target equivalent sacrifices naturalness for accuracy.

Conjunction use is genre-specific and pragmatically motivated: religion and fiction use more conjunctions than science and journalism, religion favouring negative additive and causal conjunctions, while science and journalism use few because of high assumed shared knowledge, the need for objectivity, space limits, and, in journalism, avoidance of overt causal explanation that could risk legal liability.

Adjusting patterns of conjunction to target-language norms is less straightforward than adjusting patterns of reference, because conjunction reflects the rhetoric of a text and controls its interpretation, so adjustments in translation often affect both the content and the line of argumentation.

Rechunking a text into different sections, paragraphs, or sentences is done for two main reasons: the source chunks are too long or too short relative to the target language's norm for similar material, or the target audience differs in level of specialization or age, since a specialist audience tolerates larger chunks than laymen or children.

Explicit conjunction makes a text's structure more transparent, so a more conjunctive language or text signals relations more firmly, but a less conjunctive, chattier style that appears to think aloud can be equally appropriate to its context, reflecting a difference in textual preference rather than quality.

Whether a translation follows the source text's patterns of cohesion or approximates target-language patterns depends ultimately on the purpose of the translation and how much freedom the translator feels entitled to in rechunking information and altering relation signals; following source norms minimizes change in meaning, but noticeable deviation from target chunking and signalling patterns produces a text easily identified as a foreign-sounding translation.
condition: depends on the purpose of the translation and the translator's licence to rechunk

statement: Conjunction can be a stylistic hallmark, as when a writer uses a few favourite conjunctions heavily and imprecisely to signal only that sentences are connected without indicating the nature of the connection, which poses a special problem when that hallmark of the source style is a commonplace, unremarkable feature of the target language.

Lexical cohesion is the role that vocabulary selection plays in organizing relations within a text: no lexical item is cohesive in itself, but any item can enter a cohesive relation, so lexical cohesion covers any instance in which the use of a lexical item recalls the sense of an earlier one.

Halliday and Hasan divide lexical cohesion into reiteration (repetition of an item or a synonym, superordinate, or general word, and not requiring identity of referent) and collocation (any pair of lexical items associated in the language through oppositeness, an ordered series, part-whole or co-hyponymy relations, or a history of co-occurrence).

Lexical cohesion typically operates through lexical chains that run through a text rather than through isolated pairs of words, and a main collocational chain helps establish and maintain the subject of the text, with dense networks of such ties being typical of any stretch of language.

Each occurrence of a lexical item carries its own textual history, a collocational environment built up in the course of the text that determines its instantial or text meaning, unique to that instance, so lexical networks both provide cohesion and collectively determine the sense in which each item is used.

Because the meaning of an individual lexical item is little more than a potential outside text and is realized and modified by its associations with other items, a translator analysing a text traces a web of relationships in which the importance of each item is determined by its relevance and function in the text.

It is impossible to reproduce in a target text lexical-cohesion networks identical to the source's, because a word cannot be made to mean whatever one wants, so settling for a word of slightly different meaning or associations introduces a subtle or major shift from the source's lexical chains, and such shifts occur even in non-literary text.

Lexical chains controlled by a play on an idiom's literal and non-literal meanings, sometimes tied to a visual element, often have to be sacrificed in translation, because interwoven idiom-controlled chains can be reproduced only if the target language has an idiom identical to the source idiom in both form and meaning.
condition: only reproducible when the target has an idiom identical in form and meaning

statement: The lack of ready equivalents forces strategies such as superordinate, paraphrase, or loan word, and grammatical requirements force adding, deleting, or rewording, all of which produce different lexical chains in the target text, and a paraphrase in particular cannot create the same associations as a single lexical item.

Whatever lexical and grammatical problems arise, a good translator ensures the target text displays a sufficient level of lexical cohesion in its own right, accepting that subtle or major changes are unavoidable but always avoiding the extreme of producing what appears to be a random collection of items that do not form recognizable lexical chains making sense in context.

A careful selection of lexical items collectively builds an image or impression in the reader's mind, such as items connoting sophistication, and this is lost when the target language's lexical structure lacks the same range of choices, so the target text develops its own cohesion networks that need not match the source's or trigger the same associations.

Languages differ in the level of lexical repetition they tolerate, with Arabic and Greek tolerating far higher repetition than English, and a translation can read like an original by using the target language's typical patterns of reiteration instead of copying those of the source.

The five Halliday and Hasan cohesive devices are probably common to many languages, but languages differ in which devices they prefer, how frequently they use them, and in what combinations, so pronominalization is frequent in English but rare in Japanese and Chinese, and lexical repetition is more frequent in Hebrew than in English.

Cohesion is also achieved by devices beyond the five main ones, including continuity of tense, consistency of style, and punctuation such as colons and semicolons, so unmotivated shifts in style, a common translation pitfall, can seriously disrupt the cohesion and coherence of a text.
